items.title: Phil Woods interviewed by Monk Rowe, Delaware Water Gap, PA, November 8, 1999
items.q: It was Al Cohn and myself representing the East Coast — and I don’t know how they figure these things out — and Kenny Dorham and Conte Candoli, two trumpets and tenor and alto.

ctx.x: Well you found yourself in pretty good company very quickly. Quincy Jones and Dizzy on those tours, so you were what, in your early twenties then?

Um hum. Well Birdland was also very important. I got to hanging out in Birdland and on Monday nights I worked with Jim Chapin. Jim Chapin had a band. Billy Byers did the writing for it, and Don Stratton on trumpet. And I got a little reputation and in 1956 I was invited to be part of the Birdland All-Stars. I did a thing with East Coast meets West Coast. It was Al Cohn and myself representing the East Coast — and I don’t know how they figure these things out — and Kenny Dorham and Conte Candoli, two trumpets and…

he was putting together a band for Dizzy for the Mideast tour. And so he hired me for that. And Dizzy was very important then. I mean if you’re good enough to work with Dizzy Gillespie that does wonders for opening up other doors for you.

items.title: Phil Woods — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: there was always a young band and I played with Kenny Durham

ctx.x: Yeah, but Chapin, I knew … Anyway, the dad was a drummer, a great drummer, and he had a jazz band. Billy Byers was the trombone player, I was the alto player, Don Stratton was the trumpet player. We used to work Monday nights and I got to I moved to Brooklyn which is where the Goodsteins, the people who owned Birdland, and they kind of took me under their wing. They used to bring me food and stuff like that, you know, as a kid, and tryin’ to make my way, and I was hired to do the Birdland All-Stars in 1956. But…
